title: Save the Whales!
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the "Save the Whales" movement, from the phrase's roots in the 1920s and early international whaling agreements, through the 1970s campaign (Greenpeace's Project Ahab and "mind bomb" photography, Sea Shepherd's direct action, boycotts, merchandise and pop culture), to the 1982 IWC vote and 1986 commercial whaling moratorium. They close with the continuing commercial whaling by Japan, Norway and Iceland, Japan's government subsidies and whale meat stockpiles, and modern threats like bycatch, ghost fishing and global warming. The episode ends with a listener email about battery recycling.
topics: Star Trek IV The Voyage Home

entities.name: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home

segments.title: Opening banter and the Save the Whales slogan
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the Save the Whales movement and discuss how ubiquitous the slogan was in the 1970s.

segments.title: Origins of the phrase and 1920s-30s whaling concerns
segments.summary: The phrase dates to the 1800s but took off in the 1920s, including a 1928 mammalogist meeting in Washington, DC. Early concerns echoed the bison extinction, and the League of Nations set up the Bureau of International Whaling Statistics in 1931.

segments.title: Early whaling agreements and industrial whaling
segments.summary: Hosts describe industrial whaling with cannon-fired explosive harpoons, the 1931 Geneva agreement, the 1937 agreement, and the 1946 International Whaling Commission, which lacked teeth. Post-war meat demand and a global market expanded whaling.
topics: International Agreement for the Regulation of Whaling 1937

segments.title: Whale intelligence research and Songs of the Humpback Whale
segments.summary: Navy engineer Frank Watlington's hydrophone recordings led to the 1970 album Songs of the Humpback Whale, which raised public awareness that whales were intelligent and turned them into ambassador animals.

segments.title: Album clip and the 1970s campaign launch
segments.summary: The hosts play a snippet of the album and then describe the 1971 launch of the 1970s Save the Whales campaign by the Animal Welfare Institute and Fund for Animals, including teacher outreach and boycotts.

segments.title: Boycotts, concerts and local grassroots efforts
segments.summary: A 1974 boycott of Japanese and Russian goods drew multiple groups and millions of Americans. David Bowie's 1972 benefit concert is discussed. Greenpeace joined after two years with Project Ahab. Local groups like the Connecticut Cetacean Society and Mendocino Whale Festival organized events.

segments.title: Maris Sidenstecker and Save the Whales T-shirts
segments.summary: Maris Sidenstecker sold Save the Whales T-shirts successfully from about 1974 and founded her own conservation group called Save the Whales in 1977 at age sixteen, advertising in Rolling Stone.

segments.title: Tactics: educating kids and merchandising
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the long-game approach of teaching children that whales are smart and families, plus buttons, bumper stickers and shirts as campaign tools.

segments.title: Greenpeace mind bombs and the Phyllis Cormack voyage
segments.summary: In 1975, Greenpeace's voyage aboard the Phyllis Cormack followed Russian whaling fleets off California. Close-up photographs of harpooning, termed mind bombs, ran in newspapers and drew international attention. The Whale and Dolphin Coalition in Australia took up similar tactics.

segments.title: Sea Shepherd and direct action against whaling ships
segments.summary: Paul Watson's Sea Shepherd Conservation Society rammed and sank whaling ships, including the Sierra and a ship sunk by an underwater bomb in 1980. It put bounties on pirate whaling ships and its actions raised insurance rates for whalers.

segments.title: Save the Whales in pop culture
segments.summary: Save the Whales appeared in songs by Judy Collins and Kate Bush, a 1978 board game, the 1986 Star Trek IV film, comic strips, and The Simpsons. Chuck recounts his own 1980s hippie day yearbook photo.
topics: Star Trek IV The Voyage Home

segments.title: IWC moratorium on commercial whaling (1972 to 1986)
segments.summary: The 1972 ten-year moratorium proposal was rejected, and the IWC voted again in 1982 and passed a zero catch limit for commercial whaling starting in the 1986 season, with 25 nations in favor and 7 against. It was meant to be temporary but was never lifted.

segments.title: Whale population statistics
segments.summary: Whale catch fell from about 80,000 a year in the 1960s to about 825 in 2023 by IWC estimates, with other indigenous subsistence catches. Blue, bowhead and humpback populations have recovered.

segments.title: Continuing commercial whaling by Iceland, Norway and Japan
segments.summary: Iceland, Norway and Japan objected to the moratorium and continue whaling. Japan's whaling under a scientific research exception is criticized. Whale meat consumption has fallen sharply, with a Japanese stockpile of uneaten frozen meat.

segments.title: Whaling economics and subsidies
segments.summary: Japan subsidizes whaling with about fifty million dollars a year, and nearly all of Norway's catch is exported to Japan. The global whaling industry earned about 31 million dollars in 2012, and Norway's largest company's revenue was far less than what was spent on promotion.

segments.title: Modern threats: bycatch, ghost fishing, global warming
segments.summary: Bycatch in tuna nets and ghost fishing now kill many whales, along with global warming. Conservation now has to address multiple threats, not only whaling.

segments.title: Listener mail on battery recycling and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener email from Gabby about car battery recycling exports and exploitation is read, followed by the hosts' closing banter and the show sign-off.
